sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Knowing channels is not enough — real Go codebases also use sync.WaitGroup, sync.Mutex, and select, and interviewers test these directly. The data race is one of the most common bugs in concurrent Go code, and the race detector is one of Go's best tools. For a fresher, demonstrating you understand data races and know how to detect them is a strong signal you can work safely in a concurrent codebase.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
Two patterns cover 90% of sync use cases:

- **`sync.WaitGroup` is for fan-out and wait.** Launch N goroutines, each calls `defer wg.Done()`, and `wg.Wait()` blocks until all N finish. Think of it as a counter: `Add(N)` sets the counter, each `Done()` decrements it, `Wait()` blocks until it hits zero.
- **`sync.Mutex` is for protecting shared mutable state.** Any time two goroutines could read and write the same variable, wrap the write (and ideally the read) in `mu.Lock() / mu.Unlock()`. Use `defer mu.Unlock()` immediately after `mu.Lock()` so you cannot forget to unlock even if the function returns early.
- **`select` is a channel switch.** It listens on multiple channels simultaneously and executes whichever case is ready first. If multiple cases are ready, Go picks one at random. A `default` case makes it non-blocking.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **sync.WaitGroup** — `wg.Add(1)` before each goroutine launch; `defer wg.Done()` inside the goroutine; `wg.Wait()` to block until all done; do not copy a WaitGroup after first use (pass by pointer)
- **sync.Mutex basics** — `mu.Lock()` acquires the lock (blocks if already held); `mu.Unlock()` releases; `defer mu.Unlock()` is the safe pattern to prevent forgetting unlock on early return
- **Data race definition** — two goroutines access the same memory location concurrently, at least one is a write, and there is no synchronisation between them; behaviour is undefined
- **Race detector** — `go test -race ./...` or `go run -race main.go`; the runtime instruments memory accesses and reports races with goroutine stack traces; has ~5-10x performance overhead
- **select statement basics** — `select { case v := <-ch1: ...; case ch2 <- x: ...; default: ... }` — executes first ready case; default makes it non-blocking
- **Done channel pattern** — `done := make(chan struct{})` passed to worker goroutines; `close(done)` signals all workers to stop; workers check `select { case <-done: return; default: }` in their loop

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **WaitGroup Add must come before the goroutine** — `wg.Add(1)` must be called before `go func()...`, not inside the goroutine. If the goroutine calls `wg.Add(1)`, the main goroutine may reach `wg.Wait()` before Add is called, see a count of zero, and return immediately.
- **`defer mu.Unlock()` vs calling it explicitly** — always use defer. Explicit `mu.Unlock()` at the end of a function silently fails to unlock if the function returns early (e.g., on error), causing a deadlock that is hard to reproduce.
- **The race detector is not enabled by default** — candidates who have never run `go test -race` often do not know it exists. Mentioning it proactively in an interview is a strong positive signal.
- **select with a default case is non-blocking** — `select { case v := <-ch: ...; default: }` will not block if `ch` is empty. Without `default`, it blocks until a case is ready. Interviewers ask: 'how do you do a non-blocking channel receive?'

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"For coordinating goroutines I use `sync.WaitGroup` — I call `Add` before launching each goroutine and `defer Done()` inside it, then `Wait` blocks until all finish. For protecting shared state I use `sync.Mutex` with `defer mu.Unlock()` immediately after `Lock()` so I cannot forget to release it. I always run tests with `-race` to catch data races early — the race detector instruments every memory access and reports races with full stack traces, which makes them much easier to debug than in other languages."*
